extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, students and critics of drama (writers of tragedy)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating tragic drama (classical tragedy): defines tragedy, its constituent parts, and concrete requirements for plot, character, diction, and stage elements to produce pity and fear. Useful for playwrights and literary analysts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is an imitation of an action that is serious, complete, and of a certain magnitude; in language embellished with each kind of artistic ornament; in the form of action, not of narrative; through pity and fear effecting the proper purgation (catharsis) of these emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key phrases to preserve: 'serious, complete, and of a certain magnitude'; 'language embellished' (rhythm, harmony, song); 'form of action, not of narrative'; central aim is to effect the proper purgation of pity and fear. Examples and emphasis: tragic effect arises from portrayal of actions, not merely reporting events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six constituent parts of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Every tragedy must have six parts which determine its quality — namely, Plot (mythos), Character (ethos), Diction (lexis), Thought (dianoia), Spectacle (opsis), Song (melopoiia).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These six are the canonical dimensions for composing/evaluating tragedy; some parts are the medium of imitation (song and diction), one the manner (thought), and three the objects of imitation (plot, character, spectacle). All plays contain these elements in some measure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot (mythos) as primary principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot is the imitation of the action — the arrangement or composition of the incidents — and is the first principle and most important part of tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot must be a whole (have a beginning, middle, and end), of a certain magnitude, and unified so that displacement or removal of any part disjoints the whole. It should present events according to probability or necessity (not mere chronological report). The poet should be a 'maker' of plots first rather than merely a versifier. Examples: Odyssey and Iliad constructed around a single action; avoid composing a plot as mere collection of episodes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and wholeness of plot (beginning, middle, end; unity of action)
rubrics_metrics.description: A whole plot must have a beginning (which does not follow anything by necessity), a middle (which follows and is followed), and an end (which follows something and has nothing following it). Unity of plot requires imitation of one action such that if any part is removed the whole is disturbed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unity is not identity of the hero's life; it is unity of a single action. The plot must not begin or end haphazardly; parts must be ordered and causally linked. A whole must also have appropriate magnitude (length manageable by memory and perception).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper magnitude and length of the plot
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot must be of a certain magnitude: not too small (confused in momentary perception) nor too vast (eye cannot take all in at once); the proper magnitude admits a sequence of events whereby fortune can change from good to bad or bad to good under probability or necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artistic limits (e.g., competition time) are external; the intrinsic limit is that the sequence should be perspicuous and sufficient to allow a credible change of fortune. The plot's length should be easily embraced by memory and perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid episodic (epeisodic) plots
rubrics_metrics.description: Epeisodic plots are those in which episodes succeed one another without probable or necessary sequence and are judged the worst form of plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such plots arise from bad poets' faults or from good poets catering to players (stretching plot for contests). Natural continuity must be preserved; do not string loosely-connected showpieces that lack causal/probable linkage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex vs Simple plots (use of Reversal and Recognition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plots are Simple when the change of fortune occurs without Reversal (peripeteia) or Recognition (anagnorisis). A Complex plot is one in which the change is accompanied by Reversal, Recognition, or both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A perfect tragedy should be arranged on the complex plan: reversal and recognition should arise from the internal structure of the plot (not by external contrivance) so that what follows is the necessary or probable result of what precedes. Reversal and recognition combined are especially effective in producing pity and fear (example: Oedipus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripeteia (Reversal of the Situation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peripeteia is a change by which the action veers round to its opposite, always subject to probability or necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in Oedipus a messenger intended to relieve Oedipus produces the opposite effect by revealing his identity. Reversal should feel causally or probablistically connected to preceding action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anagnorisis (Recognition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition is the change from ignorance to knowledge (or to love/hate between persons destined for good or bad fortune); the best form coincides with a Reversal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognition may involve persons or even inanimate tokens; recognition combined with reversal produces the strongest tragic effect (pity/fear). It should be grounded in the plot's internal logic; can require mutual recognitions depending on dramatic needs (e.g., Iphigenia and Orestes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pathos (tragic incident) as plot element
rubrics_metrics.description: Pathos is a destructive or painful action (death on stage, bodily agony, wounds, and the like) — a part of the plot that elicits pity and fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragic incidents are one of the essential parts of plot (with reversal and recognition). They should follow from the plot and contribute to the emotional ends of tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character (ethos) — secondary but essential
rubrics_metrics.description: Character is that in virtue of which we ascribe certain qualities to the agents; it reveals moral purpose (what a man chooses or avoids) and determines how actions are qualified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character comes second to plot: action is primary and character is subsidiary. Speeches or finely-drawn portraits alone do not substitute for a well-constructed plot. For tragic effect the protagonist should generally be neither wholly virtuous brought down to misfortune (which shocks but elicits neither pity nor fear) nor utterly villainous brought to prosperity (which is alien to tragedy), but a character of mixed quality who falls through some error (hamartia) — this produces pity and fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (dianoia) — what is said and proved
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought is the faculty of saying what is possible and pertinent in given circumstances, of proving a statement or enunciating a general truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thought performs for drama the role of political or rhetorical art: older poets used civic speech, later poets rhetorical. Thought appears where something is proved or a general maxim uttered; it should serve the action and reveal intention or reasoning of agents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction (lexis) — expression in words
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction is the expression of the meaning in words; its essence is the same both in verse and prose, including metrical arrangement (the mere metrical arrangement of the words).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diction is an important means of imitation but ranks below plot, character, and thought. Well-crafted speeches alone will not substitute for strong plot. Diction's power is operative in both metrical and non-metrical forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Song (melopoiia) — chief embellishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Song holds the chief place among the embellishments (melopoiia is the greatest of the pleasing elements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Song (choric elements, musical elements) is a central embellishment distributed in separate parts of the play (some parts rendered through verse alone, others with song). It contributes strongly to the pleasure of tragedy but must serve the overall composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle (opsis) — least artistic element
rubrics_metrics.description: Spectacle has an emotional attraction of its own but is the least artistic of the parts and is connected least with the art of poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spectacular effects depend more on stagecraft and machinist skill than on the poet; the power of tragedy should be felt even apart from representation and actors. Do not rely on spectacle alone for tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic aim: present what may happen (universality) rather than merely what happened (particular history)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet's proper function is to represent what may happen according to probability or necessity (the universal), not merely to recount what actually happened (the particular).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry is more philosophical than history because it expresses general types (how a person of a certain sort will act/speak). Therefore a poet may rearrange or invent events that are probable; even using historical material, the poet is a maker of likelihoods and types, not a chronicler.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative/performative parts of tragedy (prologue, episode, exodos, choric song parts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is divided into quantitative parts: Prologue (the whole part preceding the parodos), Episode (parts between complete choric songs), Exodos (the concluding part with no choric song after it), and Choric song (divided into Parodos — the first utterance of the Chorus — and Stasimon — a choric ode without anapaests). Also present in some plays are actors' songs from the stage and the Commos (joint lament of chorus and actors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the formal divisions for composing/analysing the structure of the play. Recognize where song and chorus occur and how episodes connect the choric songs; use these divisions to place key recognitions, reversals, and pathos moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate selection of subject-matter (not bound to received legends)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets need not rigidly adhere to traditional or received legends; fictitious names and events may be used if they are credible and give pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What matters is probability and possibility; a made-up plot or names can delight as much as known subjects. Do not feel compelled to keep to traditional myths if a newly-crafted probable action achieves the tragic aims.
